The turbine blade was made of a single crystal nickel-based superalloy called DD6, which is similar to Rene N5, PWA1484, and CMSX-4.
The turbine blade underwent a series of heat treatments, resulting in a two-phase microstructure with coherent and cuboidal γ' precipitates embedded in the γ matrix.
The TMF test rig consisted of a servo-hydraulic testing machine, a gripping fixture, a high frequency induction heater, a load synchronizer, and air/water cooling devices.
The TMF loading waveform was a trapezoidal stress/temperature wave with 35s rise/heating, 20s dwell at maximum load/temperature, and 25s fall/cooling.
The minimum temperature in the thermal cycle was 200°C.
The TMF test was conducted under load control with a stress ratio R = 0.05.
The experiment was terminated after 325 cycles when a crack emerged at the suction side near the trailing edge.
No cracks were observed at the film-cooling holes or other locations on the specimen.
The crack surface was almost perpendicular to the loading direction.
The crack propagated from the inside wall towards the outside, as evidenced by the variation in oxidation layer thickness and fatigue striations.
The crack propagation life was estimated to be 64 cycles, accounting for 19.7% of the total fatigue life.
The finite element simulation results showed that the pin-fin fillet near the trailing edge suffered the most severe TMF damage.
The maximum accumulated slip strain at the pin-fin fillet was 54.8% higher than at the film-cooling holes.
Increasing the pin-fin fillet radius and lowering the temperature in that region were suggested to improve the TMF resistance.
The high frequency induction heating system provided convenient temperature control and a high heating rate.
